writing.prompt: Show the calculation for 16 and 24 recombinant offspring with 90 and 70 parental offspring. Include an interpretation.
writing.model: Total = 16 + 24 + 90 + 70 = 200. Recombinants = 40. Frequency = 40/200 × 100% = 20%, suggesting about 20 map units in a simple short-interval model. It is an estimate based on the scored loci.

writing.prompt: Explain why a map unit is not a universal physical DNA length and why two-locus frequencies have limits.
writing.model: Map units reflect recombination probability. Recombination varies across chromosome regions and organisms, so no fixed base-pair conversion applies universally. Multiple crossovers can be undetected, and two-locus recombinant frequency approaches the independent limit of 50%.

videos.title: Recombination frequency and chromosome maps — video support
videos.purpose: Calculate recombination frequency, construct simple maps and distinguish map distance from a universal physical base-pair distance.
videos.fallback: Suppose A–B is 6 map units, B–C is 14 and A–C is 20 in a simple additive map. Since 6 + 14 = 20, B lies between A and C. Either A—6—B—14—C or its reversed orientation expresses the same relative order. Two distances alone may leave more than one order possible. Place the genes tentatively and ask what additional comparison would distinguish the alternatives. Do not invent a third distance merely to finish the drawing.
